clue.text: Andersen's swansong?

parts.note: Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale about a misfit cygnet who grows into a swan is read as a 'swan song' by him

explanation.surface: A question about the last work of the Danish storyteller Hans Christian Andersen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swansong' normally means a final performance; here it is read literally as Andersen's story whose hero turns out to be a swan.
explanation.definitionFit: Andersen's tale tells of a scorned grey bird that grows into a beautiful swan, so it is literally his song of a swan.

clue.text: An old London coach, per- L haps, towards the back of dramatic scenery

definitions.text: An old London coach, per- L haps
towards the back of dramatic scenery

explanation.surface: A description of a vintage carriage parked at the rear of a theatre set.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'per- L haps' is the word 'perhaps' broken across a line. A stagecoach travelling 'up' to London could be called an up stage; in theatre, upstage is the area furthest from the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage directions call the rear of the set, away from the audience, up stage; a stagecoach heading to the capital is going up.

clue.text: Seasonal flower gone with the wind

definitions.text: Seasonal flower gone with the wind

parts.words: Seasonal flower gone with the wind
parts.note: a tide is a periodic flow of the sea, here one running in the same direction the wind blows, to leeward

explanation.surface: A bloom of the season blown away by a gale, with a nod to the film title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is read as something that flows, the sea, not a bloom; 'gone with the wind' means moving the same way as the wind, to leeward.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors name a tidal stream running the same way as the wind after the sheltered, downwind side of a vessel.

clue.text: A dogged ill humour

parts.note: read as an illness that dogs suffer, and also as an old word for a bad mood or disordered temperament

explanation.surface: A stubborn bout of grumpiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogged' looks like 'persistent' but means 'affecting dogs': the canine viral disease; the word once also meant a disordered humour or temper.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a contagious viral disease of dogs and, in older English, a bad temper or disturbed state of mind.

clue.text: Oncer "bewitched

indicators.note: something bewitched is put under a spell and transformed, so these letters are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone seen only once has fallen under a spell.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearranging ONCER under the signal 'bewitched' gives the word for an old hag, the sort of figure who casts spells.
explanation.definitionFit: A withered old woman of folklore, often pictured as a witch casting enchantments.

clue.text: The solo arrangement Basutoland has come to

indicators.note: an arrangement of the words puts their letters into a new order, as a musician arranges a piece

explanation.surface: A musical arrangement of a solo that a southern African country has reached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrangement' suggests music, but it signals the anagram of THE SOLO. 'Has come to' links: Basutoland became this kingdom at independence in 1966.
explanation.definitionFit: The British protectorate of Basutoland took its present name when it gained independence in 1966.

clue.text: Ingenuousness of native development absorbing East

indicators.note: one piece soaks up another, taking it inside
a development of the word reworks its letters into something new

explanation.surface: The innocence of a local person grows as they take in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Development' turns NATIVE into NAIVTE, and 'absorbing' puts E (East) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingenuousness is innocent simplicity, a lack of worldly experience or guile.

clue.text: How often we feel closest to being wed?

definitions.text: How often we feel closest to being wed?

parts.words: How often we feel closest to being wed?
parts.note: 'wed' is read as the start of the name of the midweek day, so the day nearest to it in the calendar is meant, weekly

explanation.surface: A question about how frequently a couple feel nearest to marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wed' looks like marriage but is the short form of Wednesday; the day just before it comes round once a week.
explanation.definitionFit: The day immediately preceding Wednesday recurs weekly, so this phrase answers 'how often'.

clue.text: Afterthought woven into unusual verse for evening service

indicators.note: the afterthought is woven into the verse and the whole made unusual, so all the letters are mixed together in a new order

parts.note: PS, postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: A postscript worked into odd poetry for a church service at dusk.
explanation.walkthrough: PS (postscript) and VERSE form one pool of letters, rearranged under 'woven into unusual'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vespers is the evening prayer service of the Christian liturgy.

clue.text: Turning out for an excursion round Swiss capital

indicators.note: one piece goes round another, enclosing it

parts.note: an outing is a trip or excursion

indicators.note: the capital, or head, letter of the word is its first

explanation.surface: Taking a trip around Bern, the Swiss capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swiss capital' suggests Bern, but means the first letter of Swiss, S, which 'round' puts inside OUTING.
explanation.definitionFit: Ousting someone is turning them out, expelling them from a place or post.

clue.text: Just for fun having a shot at naming the object of the chase

parts.note: guessing is trying to name something without knowing
game is the animals hunted in a chase

explanation.surface: A light-hearted attempt at identifying the quarry in a hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a parlour pastime played purely for amusement.
explanation.definitionFit: A parlour pastime in which players try to identify something, played purely for amusement.

clue.text: Convert to cash each pound within increment

parts.note: a rise is an increase, an increment
L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for pound

explanation.surface: A banker's instruction to turn assets into money, a pound at a time in each pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: EA and L go 'within' RISE to make R-EAL-ISE.
explanation.definitionFit: To realise assets is to sell them and turn them into money.

clue.text: This sort of view's 'the abse lute limit

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain opinion is the furthest anyone can go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abse lute' is the word 'absolute' split by the printing. An extreme view is a radical opinion; the extreme is the furthest possible point.
explanation.definitionFit: Radical opinions are called extreme views, and the noun means the furthest point or utmost degree.

clue.text: The subject of an egoist's personal objective

parts.note: me is the objective case of the personal pronoun I, the word an egoist cares about most

explanation.surface: A question about the topic that a self-centred person aims at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Objective' looks like a goal but is the grammatical case: ME is the objective form of I, the egoist's favourite word.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic or subject of a talk or essay is its central idea.

clue.text: Old English prisons rebuilt for murderers

indicators.note: the building is put back together in a different order

explanation.surface: Ancient English jails reconstructed to house killers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rebuilt' rearranges OE (Old English) plus PRISONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Murderers who kill with toxic substances, such as arsenic.

clue.text: Some teeth put in first contract

parts.note: a denture is a set of artificial teeth

explanation.surface: Someone getting false teeth fitted before signing an agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put ... first' tells you to place IN before DENTURE.
explanation.definitionFit: An indenture is a formal agreement, especially one binding an apprentice to a master.

clue.text: Being in love with love, given eye-opener in the finish

parts.note: the end is the finish
amour is a love or love affair

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone in love with love itself who gets a surprise at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eye-opener' looks like a surprise, but gives the first letter of eye, E. AMOUR and E go 'in' END.
explanation.definitionFit: To be enamoured is to be infatuated, charmed or in love.

clue.text: Pardon for Volunteers running amok in Lincoln?

parts.note: Abe is the nickname of US President Abraham Lincoln

indicators.note: running wild breaks things up into disorder

parts.note: VOLS is a short form of volunteers

explanation.surface: Asking for forgiveness for volunteer soldiers rampaging in the English city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lincoln' looks like the English city but is President Abraham (Abe) Lincoln; SOLV, from VOLS 'running amok', goes 'in' ABE.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve is to pardon, free someone from guilt or blame.

clue.text: Go over the edge where a Nanny changed the baby

definitions.text: where a Nanny changed the baby

explanation.surface: A nanny changing nappies with the baby across her knees.
explanation.walkthrough: A nanny changes a baby across her knees: the baby is over the lap. As one word, the verb means extend beyond an edge onto something else.
explanation.definitionFit: To extend past a border onto another surface; and a baby being changed lies across the knees.

clue.text: A girl finds a country between two points

indicators.note: one piece sits between the others

parts.note: S and N, south and north, are two compass points
USA is the United States of America

explanation.surface: A young woman discovers a nation lying between two places.
explanation.walkthrough: USA goes 'between' the compass points S and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Susan is a common female first name.

clue.text: Though a chapel in Italy it's put up within Latin environment

parts.note: sine is Latin for without, and without means outside, so it surrounds

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a word up writes it from bottom to top, backwards

explanation.surface: A tourist note that a chapel in Italy has been built within a Latin setting.
explanation.walkthrough: ITS 'put up' becomes STI, which goes 'within' SINE. The chapel is the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sistine Chapel in the Vatican, famous for Michelangelo's ceiling.

clue.text: Go forth from a raised front in door?

definitions.text: Go forth from a raised front in door?

parts.words: Go forth from a raised front in door?
parts.note: read as leaving a house by going over the raised slab in front of the door

explanation.surface: Leaving a building by way of a raised doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The raised slab in front of a door is a step; to leave a house you go out over it, and the phrase means go out.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means to go outside or leave briefly, and a doorstep is a raised front.

clue.text: Scatters Hellish charms, we're told

indicators.note: what we are told is heard spoken, so the words sound like the solution

parts.note: Dis is the classical god and realm of the underworld, so hellish charms are Dis spells

explanation.surface: Someone drives off charms from hell, so it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: Dis is the Roman underworld; 'Dis spells', spoken, gives the word for drives away.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispel is to drive away or scatter fears, doubts or a crowd.

clue.text: She might write a romance or saga with novel beginning

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A woman who writes love stories or epic tales with a fresh start.
explanation.walkthrough: Françoise Sagan, French author of 'Bonjour Tristesse'. SAGA plus the 'beginning' of novel, N.
explanation.definitionFit: Françoise Sagan was a French novelist whose books dealt with love affairs.

clue.text: Pen's output laid by for a future 1 across?

definitions.text: Pen's output laid by for a future 1 across?

parts.words: Pen's output laid by for a future 1 across?
parts.note: a pen is a female swan; her output is eggs, laid in a nest, from which a cygnet will hatch

explanation.surface: A writer's work set aside for a later piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a writing tool but is a female swan, and 'laid by' means saved: savings put by for the future.
explanation.definitionFit: Money set aside as savings for the future; and a swan's egg in its nest awaits a cygnet.

clue.text: Noel's blazer takes some matching…

parts.note: Noel is Christmas, and the blazer is a burning fire log, not a jacket

explanation.surface: A man called Noel has a jacket that is hard to match with trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blazer' looks like a jacket and Noel a man; it is a large log burned on the hearth at Christmas, needing a match to light.
explanation.definitionFit: A large log traditionally burned on the hearth at Christmas, or a chocolate cake shaped like one.

clue.text: … even for those who wish to dress the same

definitions.text: for those who wish to dress the same

explanation.surface: Clothing advice for people who like to match each other.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to the matching of the previous clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means consistent and level; as a noun it is the identical outfit worn by a team or force.

clue.text: An oceanographer's profound concern

explanation.surface: A marine scientist's serious worry.
explanation.walkthrough: An oceanographer studies the deep sea, so their concern is literally in the deep.
explanation.definitionFit: Great curiosity or concern; and a scientist of the seas is interested in the ocean depths.
